# Control Narrative: Sanitary Lift Station LS-12

Draft for review. Items marked **[CONFIRM]** are assumptions I added to fill gaps in the operations input. Each needs an owner's decision before programming and FAT.

## 1. Purpose and scope

LS-12 pumps wastewater from a 3.0 m deep wet well using two submersible pumps, P-121 and P-122. Each pump is sized for 100% of design flow and is driven by a VFD. The station operates automatically on wet well level. It must never reach the 2.8 m overflow elevation, because an overflow discharges to a creek and is a permit violation. Where this narrative has to trade off convenience against overflow prevention, overflow prevention wins.

## 2. Equipment and instruments

| Tag | Description | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| P-121, P-122 | Submersible pumps on VFDs | 100% duty each |
| LIT-121 | Submersible pressure transducer | 0-3.0 m, 4-20 mA |
| LSL-121 | Low level float | 0.4 m, pump protection |
| LSHH-121 | High-high level float | 2.6 m, backup high level |
| HS-121, HS-122 | Hand-Off-Auto switches at MCC | One per pump |
| ATS / standby generator | Automatic power transfer | Status inputs to PLC |
| PLC | Station controller | Reports to SCADA over licensed radio |

## 3. Level reference and setpoints

All levels are in metres above the wet well floor, as measured by LIT-121.

| Elevation (m) | Function | Type |
|---|---|---|
| 3.0 | Wet well top / transducer span limit | Reference |
| 2.8 | Overflow to creek | **Permit violation, never reach** |
| 2.6 | LSHH-121 (float) | Backup high-high alarm, forced pump run |
| 2.3 | LAH-121 high level alarm | Alarm only |
| 2.0 | Lag pump start | Adjustable |
| 1.6 | Lead pump start, ramp begins at 45 Hz | Adjustable |
| 1.6 to 2.0 | Lead speed ramp, 45 to 60 Hz | |
| 0.6 | Lead pump stop | Adjustable |
| 0.4 | LSL-121 (float) | Low level cutout, hardwired |

All analog setpoints are operator-adjustable from SCADA and the local HMI, with range checks. They must keep this ordering: LSL < stop < lead start < lag start < alarm < LSHH. The PLC rejects any entry that violates it.

**Design observations to resolve before FAT:**
1. The headroom between LSHH-121 (2.6 m) and overflow (2.8 m) is only 0.2 m. That leaves very little reaction time if the primary level and pumps have both failed. Consider raising the priority of the alarm callout, or moving LSHH-121 lower, for example to 2.5 m. **[CONFIRM]**
2. The span of 0.2 m between the 2.3 m alarm and the 2.6 m LSHH is small, and the alarm sits above the lag start. If level reaches 2.3 m with both pumps running, the pumps are not keeping up. This is the correct meaning of the alarm.
3. Confirm with the pump manufacturer that the 0.6 m stop level gives adequate submergence at 45 Hz, and that 45 Hz gives adequate velocity in the force main (scour and minimum flow).

## 4. Operating modes

### 4.1 HOA switch (per pump)
- **OFF:** The pump is stopped and cannot start from the PLC. The PLC treats it as unavailable.
- **HAND:** The pump runs from the MCC, bypassing the PLC auto sequence, at a fixed local speed of 60 Hz **[CONFIRM]**. Hardwired protections stay active: LSL-121 low level cutout, VFD faults, motor protection. The PLC reads the HAND status, alarms it, and removes the pump from the lead/lag rotation.
- **AUTO:** The PLC controls the pump per Section 5.

If one pump is not in AUTO, or is faulted, the other pump becomes lead and the only available pump. Section 5.5 covers this.

### 4.2 Station-level behavior
The PLC executes all auto control locally. A loss of radio or SCADA does not affect pump control.

## 5. Automatic control sequence

### 5.1 Run permissives (per pump)
A pump may be commanded to run in AUTO only if all of these are true:
- HOA is in AUTO.
- The VFD reports no fault and is ready.
- LSL-121 is not in the low-level state (level above 0.4 m).
- No motor protection trip is active (seal leak, motor over-temperature, and similar, as supplied). **[CONFIRM the list]**
- The pump is not in a minimum off-time or restart delay (Section 5.7).

LSL-121 is hardwired in the run permissive chain, independent of the PLC, so that it stops the pumps even if the PLC fails. **[CONFIRM the hardwiring approach.]**

### 5.2 Lead pump start and stop
- When LIT-121 level rises to **1.6 m** or above, the PLC starts the lead pump.
- The lead pump runs until level falls to **0.6 m** or below, then stops.
- Once started, the pump stays running between 0.6 m and 1.6 m. It does not stop just because level drops below 1.6 m.
- Starts and stops use the setpoints directly. There is no additional deadband, because the 1.0 m span is the hysteresis.

### 5.3 Lead pump speed
- Speed reference starts at **45 Hz** when the lead pump starts at 1.6 m.
- Between 1.6 m and 2.0 m, the speed reference follows a linear function of level:

  `Hz = 45 + (level − 1.6) × (60 − 45) / (2.0 − 1.6)`

  This gives 45 Hz at 1.6 m, 52.5 Hz at 1.8 m, and 60 Hz at 2.0 m.
- Above 2.0 m, the lead speed is held at 60 Hz.
- Below 1.6 m (pump-down), the lead speed is held at 45 Hz until the stop level.
- The PLC limits the speed reference to a rate of change of **[CONFIRM, suggest 1 Hz/s]**, and the VFD's own accel/decel ramps apply in addition. The speed reference is clamped to 45-60 Hz.

### 5.4 Lag pump start and stop
- If level rises to **2.0 m** with the lead pump running, the PLC starts the lag pump.
- The lag pump runs at **60 Hz** **[CONFIRM: the input does not state lag speed]**.
- Lag stop: the lag pump stops when level falls to **1.2 m** **[CONFIRM: the input gives no lag stop]**. The lead pump continues to 0.6 m. If operations prefers, both pumps may stop together at 0.6 m, but a separate lag stop reduces simultaneous-stop surge in the force main.
- Lag start uses the same permissives as 5.1. If the lag pump is not available, the alarm in 5.6 applies and the lead pump keeps running at 60 Hz.

### 5.5 Alternation
- Lead/lag assignment alternates **every pump cycle**. A cycle is one complete start-to-stop of the lead pump. At each lead pump stop, the PLC swaps the roles, so the previous lag becomes lead on the next call.
- If only one pump is available (the other is in OFF/HAND, faulted, or locked out), that pump is lead on every cycle and alternation is suspended. The PLC raises an alarm, "Single pump operation."
- If the lead pump fails to start or trips while running, the other pump is called immediately as lead and a fault alarm is raised. The failed pump is locked out until the fault is cleared and reset.
- Role assignment is stored in retentive memory so it survives a PLC restart or power loss.
- An operator-selectable override (SCADA) lets operations force P-121 or P-122 as lead. **[CONFIRM if wanted]**

### 5.6 High level response
- **2.3 m, LAH-121:** High level alarm, to SCADA and callout. If the lag pump is available but not running, the PLC commands it to start as well. This should already have happened at 2.0 m. If both pumps are running at 60 Hz and level still rises, the alarm indicates inflow exceeds capacity or a pump or force main problem.
- **2.6 m, LSHH-121:** Hardwired float input to the PLC, and also wired so it can force each pump to run through the VFD in AUTO **[CONFIRM design: hardwired relay logic or PLC only]**. Action:
  - Annunciate a critical alarm with highest-priority callout.
  - Command all available pumps to run at 60 Hz regardless of the lead/lag logic.
  - Pumps run until level falls to the normal lead stop, with the LSHH-121 alarm latched until acknowledged.
  - LSHH-121 overrides the minimum off-time delay, but not the VFD fault, motor protection, or LSL-121 interlocks.
  - HOA in HAND or OFF is respected, so the alarm tells operations to respond locally.

### 5.7 Pump protection timers
All values are adjustable. **[CONFIRM the values.]**
- Minimum run time: 30 s, except when stopping on the low level cutout.
- Minimum off time and starts per hour limit: confirm with the pump and VFD manufacturers. Suggest 5 min between starts of the same pump and at most 6 starts per hour. Alternation spreads starts between pumps.
- Pump failure to run: if the PLC commands a run and the VFD does not report running within 10 s, the pump is faulted.
- Lag start delay after lead start: 5 s, to avoid simultaneous starts.

## 6. Instrument failure handling

### 6.1 LIT-121 failure
LIT-121 is considered failed if the signal is below 3.5 mA or above 20.5 mA, or if the reading is frozen or jumps implausibly. **[CONFIRM the rate-of-change check.]** On failure:
- Raise "LIT-121 fail" as a high-priority alarm.
- Switch to float-based backup control:
  - LSHH-121 (2.6 m) calls for pumps. All available pumps run at 60 Hz, alternating the lead pump each cycle.
  - LSL-121 (0.4 m) stops the pumps.
- Because the backup floats start pumps only 0.2 m below overflow, backup mode is a last resort. **Recommend adding a mid-level float, such as one near the 1.6 m lead start, so a failed transmitter does not leave the station running on the overflow margin. [CONFIRM]**
- When LIT-121 returns to a valid signal for 10 s, the PLC resumes normal control. A hold-on-fault latch keeps the station in backup mode until an operator acknowledges, to avoid chatter. **[CONFIRM]**

### 6.2 Float disagreement
- LSL-121 low while LIT-121 reads above 1.0 m: alarm "LSL-121 / LIT-121 disagree."
- LSHH-121 high while LIT-121 reads below 2.0 m: alarm "LSHH-121 / LIT-121 disagree."
- LIT-121 above 2.6 m while LSHH-121 is not tripped: same alarm. In that case the PLC still applies the LSHH response from the analog value.

## 7. Power failure and generator

- On loss of utility power, the ATS starts the standby generator and transfers load. The PLC receives status inputs: utility power OK, generator running, ATS in the emergency position, generator fault, and low fuel. **[CONFIRM the available signals.]** The PLC, instruments, and radio are powered from a UPS or DC supply so that they ride through the transfer.
- After transfer, the PLC applies a restart delay and a staggered pump start, with at least 10 s between pump starts. **[CONFIRM against generator sizing.]**
- If the generator can only support one pump at a time, the PLC limits to one running pump while on generator power. **This is a design decision needed from the electrical engineer, because a single pump must then keep up with the inflow. [CONFIRM]**
- On generator power the PLC reports "Running on generator." If the generator fails to start, or fuel is low, a critical alarm is sent immediately because the station will not be able to pump, and the overflow risk is real.
- Loss of power to the station without generator transfer is a critical alarm, sent by the radio's backup supply.
- On return of utility power, the ATS retransfers after its own timer, and the PLC applies the same restart sequence.

## 8. Alarms

| Tag | Condition | Priority |
|---|---|---|
| LSHH-121 | Level at or above 2.6 m (float) | Critical |
| LAH-121 | Level at or above 2.3 m | High |
| LSL-121 | Level at or below 0.4 m (float) | High |
| LAL-121 | Level below 0.5 m **[CONFIRM]** while pumping not expected | Medium |
| LIT-121 FAIL | Out of range or frozen signal | High |
| P-121/122 FAULT | VFD or motor protection | High |
| P-121/122 FAIL TO RUN | Commanded but not running | High |
| P-121/122 NOT IN AUTO | HOA in HAND or OFF | Medium |
| SINGLE PUMP | Only one pump available | High |
| POWER FAIL / ON GENERATOR | ATS status | High |
| GENERATOR FAULT / FAIL TO START | | Critical |
| COMMS FAIL | SCADA radio communications lost | Medium |
| PLC / UPS FAULT | Includes UPS on battery | High |
| FLOAT / LIT DISAGREE | See 6.2 | Medium |
| PUMP RUNTIME / STARTS HIGH | Diagnostic | Low |

Latching and acknowledgement: LSHH, pump faults, and fail-to-run latch until reset. Others auto-clear. All alarms and events are time-stamped in the PLC and sent to SCADA. Unacknowledged critical alarms are re-annunciated periodically. **[CONFIRM the callout path.]**

## 9. SCADA and communications

- The PLC reports over licensed radio. **[CONFIRM the protocol, such as DNP3 or Modbus, and the poll rate.]**
- Reported points: level, pump status, speed, current, running hours, start counts, HOA status, alarms, power and generator status, and setpoints. The PLC time-stamps events and buffers them if the radio is down. **[CONFIRM report by exception.]**
- Commands from SCADA: setpoint changes within limits, lead pump selection override, and alarm acknowledge. **[CONFIRM if remote start/stop is allowed.]** The narrative recommends no remote start of pumps in HAND, and no remote bypass of any interlock.
- On loss of communications the station continues in local automatic control without change. A comms failure alarm is generated at SCADA by a heartbeat timeout. Since radio is the only alarm path, the loss of comms with a high-level event is a significant overflow risk. Consider a second independent alarm path, such as a cellular dialer or a beacon. **[CONFIRM]**

## 10. FAT test plan (summary)

Simulate LIT-121 with a mA source. Simulate floats with switches. Simulate VFD feedback with I/O simulation. Record pass/fail and measured values.

| # | Test | Expected result |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Level rises to 1.59 m, then 1.6 m | No start below 1.6 m. Lead starts at 1.6 m at 45 Hz. |
| 2 | Level 1.8 m | Lead speed 52.5 Hz (±0.5). |
| 3 | Level 2.0 m | Lead 60 Hz, lag starts at 60 Hz. |
| 4 | Level above 2.0 m, then falls | Lead speed holds 60 Hz down to 2.0, then follows the ramp to 1.6, then holds 45 Hz. (Confirm intended behavior on the falling side.) |
| 5 | Level falls to 1.2 m | Lag stops. |
| 6 | Level falls to 0.6 m | Lead stops. |
| 7 | Repeat 5 full cycles | Lead role swaps each cycle: P-121, P-122, P-121... |
| 8 | Role stored after PLC power cycle | Lead assignment retained. |
| 9 | Level 2.3 m | LAH alarm at SCADA. Lag started if not running. |
| 10 | LSHH-121 at 2.6 m | Critical alarm, all available pumps run at 60 Hz, latched. |
| 11 | LSL-121 at 0.4 m with pump running | Pumps stop, independent of PLC (verify with PLC in stop). |
| 12 | HOA to OFF on one pump | That pump is unavailable. Other pump becomes lead. Single-pump alarm. |
| 13 | HOA to HAND | Pump runs locally, alarm, removed from rotation, LSL still stops it. |
| 14 | VFD fault on lead during run | Lag takes over as lead immediately. Fault alarm. |
| 15 | Fail-to-run (no run feedback) | Fault after 10 s, other pump called. |
| 16 | LIT-121 at 2 mA, then at 22 mA | LIT FAIL alarm, backup float mode. |
| 17 | LIT-121 frozen | Detected per setting. |
| 18 | Float / LIT disagreement | Alarms per 6.2. |
| 19 | Setpoint ordering violation entered at HMI | Rejected. |
| 20 | Utility power loss, ATS transfer | Staggered restart, generator status, alarms. |
| 21 | Generator fail to start | Critical alarm. |
| 22 | Radio link disconnected | Station continues in auto. Comms fail alarm at SCADA. Events buffered and uploaded on reconnect. |
| 23 | Min run / min off / starts-per-hour timers | Enforced, except where overridden by LSHH. |
| 24 | Both pumps unavailable at high level | Critical alarms. No pump commands issued. |

## 11. Open items for the project team

1. Lag pump speed and lag stop level (not in the operations input).
2. Hand-mode speed and protections.
3. LSHH-121 position (2.6 m) relative to overflow (2.8 m), and the case for a mid-level backup float.
4. Hardwired versus PLC implementation of the LSL and LSHH interlocks.
5. Generator capacity: one or two pumps at once.
6. Alarm callout path and a second communication path.
7. Pump manufacturer's limits: minimum submergence, minimum speed, starts per hour.
8. Radio protocol and SCADA tag names.

If you can send the answers to items 1-7, I can finalize the document and produce the I/O list and tag table.
